profile.campus: Google Central Ohio (New Albany / Columbus-Lockbourne / Lancaster), OH
profile.address: Babbitt Road, New Albany, Plain Township, Franklin County, OH 43004 (5)
profile.reading:
This building is part of Google's New Albany, Ohio data center campus, mapped on Babbitt Road in Plain Township, and carries the informational label NBY-1 in this registry's underlying mapping data, not independently confirmed against a Google-published building index this session; the county field in this registry's underlying data lists Licking County for this row, though the coordinate falls within the New Albany campus area near the Franklin/Licking county line. As the lowest-numbered code among the NBY-series buildings tracked in this registry, this may correspond to Google's original New Albany facility, but that inference is not confirmed against a Google-published source this session.

Google's cloud infrastructure operates as a business of Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ: GOOGL/GOOG, SEC CIK 0001652044), headquartered at 1600 Amphitheatre Parkway, Mountain View, California. Google's own Ohio data center location page, fetched fresh this session, states the company broke ground in New Albany in 2019 and has since invested more than $20 billion in the state across New Albany, Lancaster, and Columbus, generating $21.7 billion in Ohio economic activity in 2025 and contributing over $16 million in philanthropic giving since 2006.

New Albany has become the anchor of Ohio's central data center corridor since Google broke ground there in 2019, though Google's own public materials describe its New Albany footprint in aggregate rather than naming individual buildings, addresses, or per-building capacity figures.

American Electric Power (AEP Ohio) is the principal electric utility serving most of the New Albany and Columbus-area data center market, and has filed with Ohio regulators for new large-load electric tariff structures in response to rapidly growing data center demand in the corridor. New Albany's community authority has used tax-increment financing agreements, and Ohio's state-level data center sales and use tax abatement program, to help anchor the cluster's continued growth alongside Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon Web Services campuses tracked elsewhere in this registry.

profile.regional_context: Central Ohio's data center corridor, anchored by New Albany, has grown since 2019 into one of the state's largest technology investment clusters, also hosting large campuses for Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon Web Services, all separately tracked in this registry. American Electric Power (AEP Ohio) is the principal electric utility serving most of the New Albany and Columbus-area data center market, and has filed for new large-load electric tariff structures in response to rapidly growing data center demand. Ohio's data center-specific sales and use tax abatement program, and New Albany's own community authority tax-increment financing agreements, have been credited by state and local officials with anchoring the cluster's growth.

reading.body:
Google does not publish individual building capacity for NBY-1 or any site in its New Albany/Columbus-area campus spanning Franklin, Licking, and Fairfield counties. The company discloses only aggregate state-level investment figures, so the power and rack count of this facility cannot be determined from public sources. The $1.7 billion combined investment across the Columbus and Lancaster, Ohio campuses signals major hyperscale commitment to the region alongside AWS and Meta, but this campus cannot yet be ranked by capacity.

Ohio has 76 mapped data center facilities, but only 8 publish power specifications totaling 60.4 MW. NBY-1 cannot be placed in that ranking because its capacity is not disclosed. The absence of a figure does not indicate the facility is small; it reflects Google's policy of withholding individual building specs.

For readers assessing whether this campus matters to AI, the lack of published capacity makes it impossible to judge its contribution to grid constraint or accelerator density from public data alone. The regional context shows Google is scaling substantially in this corridor, but the binding constraint question for this site cannot be answered without either operator disclosure or independent measurement.
